## QUESTION 1

__Write an SQL query that pulls the tables you need into a polars dataframe using nothing more than SELECT and FROM statements. Then, use python polars to identify the top 10 players with the longest Major League Baseball careers. Include their playerID, first_name, last_name, and career_length__

I chose the people table because it had a debut game date and final game date for every player, which I felt was the best way to determine the length of their career. I subtracted the debut game date from the final game date to get the duration in days, then divided the duration by 365.25 to get the duration in years. Nick Altrock has the longest career of 35.21 years starting in 1898, and all but two of the longest careers started before 1905. There are two that started after but the trend seems to be that modern players don't play as long as those from over 100 years ago. 

```{python}
q1 = "SELECT playerID, nameFirst, nameLast, debut_date, finalgame_date FROM people"

people_df = pl.read_database(q1, con)

people_df


longest_careers = (
    people_df.with_columns(
        career_length=(
            pl.col("finalgame_date").str.to_date() - pl.col("debut_date").str.to_date()
        )
    )
    .with_columns(
        career_length_years=(
            (pl.col("career_length").dt.total_days(fractional=True) / 365.25).round(2)
        ),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("career_length_years").is_not_null())
    .select(
        [
            "playerID",
            "nameFirst",
            "nameLast",
            "debut_date",
            "finalgame_date",
            "career_length_years",
        ]
    )
    .sort("career_length_years", descending=True)
    .head(10)
)

longest_careers
```

__Write an SQL query that pulls the tables you need into a polars dataframe. Then, use python polars to create a summary table showing the average salary for each position (e.g., pitcher, catcher, outfielder). Position information can be found in the fielding table in the POS column. Include position, average_salary, total_players, highest_salary__

As someone who knows nothing about baseball I was surprised to find out that first basemen get paid the most by a large margin. I had assumed it was pitchers, but they're 3rd to last. It is odd that pitchers are tied for the highest individual salary in that case, but they also have by FAR the most players which was also surprising to me. Overall there was quite a bit of unexpected information here. The outfield having almost 3x the player count of all the other positions except pitchers makes perfect sense given that the outfield is really 3 positions in a trenchcoat. 

```{python}
# Pulling in tables
q2="SELECT * FROM fielding"
q3="SELECT * FROM fieldingofsplit"
q4="SELECT * FROM salaries"

df_fielding = pl.read_database(q2,con, infer_schema_length=None)
df_salaries = pl.read_database(q4, con, infer_schema_length=None)

df_salary_positions = df_fielding.select(["playerID","yearID","teamID","POS","G","GS"]).join(df_salaries, on=["playerID","yearID","teamID"], how="inner", suffix="_new_new")

df_appearances = pl.read_database("SELECT * FROM appearances", con, infer_schema_length=None)

df_total_appearances = df_appearances.group_by(["playerID", "yearID","teamID"]).agg(total_games = pl.col("G_defense").sum()).select(["playerID","yearID","teamID","total_games"]).sort("playerID")

df_appearances_salary = df_salary_positions.join(df_total_appearances, on=["playerID","yearID","teamID"], how="left")

df_appearances_proportion = df_appearances_salary.with_columns(pos_proportion = pl.col("G")/pl.col("total_games")).sort(
        ["playerID", "yearID", "pos_proportion"],
        descending=[False, False, True]
    ).unique(
        subset=["playerID", "yearID", "teamID"],
        keep="first",
        maintain_order=True
    ).select(["playerID", "yearID", "POS", "G", "pos_proportion","salary"])

df_avg_pos_salaries = df_appearances_proportion.group_by("POS").agg(average_salary_millions = (pl.col("salary").mean() / 1000000), total_players = pl.col("playerID").n_unique(), highest_salary_millions = pl.col("salary").max()/1000000).sort("average_salary_millions",descending=True)

df_avg_pos_salaries

```
